facts.label: Rotation period
facts.value: 5.34 hours

controls.label: Natural color
controls.notes: DLR natural-color composite from Dawn’s 650, 550, and 430 nm filters, calibrated and photometrically corrected. Very bright terrain is clipped to white in the published image. Where the color mosaic has no coverage, the HAMO clear-filter mosaic shows in gray. Local shadows and channel-registration artifacts may remain.

controls.label: Clear-filter photography
controls.notes: Dawn low-altitude clear-filter photographs in the published DLR mosaic. Sunlit crater walls, shadows and mosaic seams belong to the observations. The source is 20 m/pixel; this simplified display is coarser. The north, which the low orbit never saw lit, takes the 60 m/pixel HAMO mosaic; exact black pixels are withheld by the fill heuristic and drawn as the gray grid.

controls.label: HAMO photography
controls.notes: Dawn high-altitude clear-filter photographs in the published DLR mosaic of May 2013, HAMO-1 for the south (2011) and HAMO-2 for the north (June to July 2012). It is the only Dawn product that reaches the north pole, photographed under low northern-spring sun, so the northernmost band is dim. Original illumination and seams remain; exact black is withheld and drawn as the gray grid.

controls.label: Spectral ratios
controls.notes: DLR’s published Clementine-style composite of photometrically corrected Dawn images: red is 749/438 nm, green is 749/917 nm, and blue is 438/749 nm. Colors emphasize spectral differences; they are not natural color or a mineral-abundance measurement. Original seams and color fringes remain. Exact black is treated as likely fill, so some dark observations may also be withheld; gaps use the gray grid.

controls.label: Elevation
controls.notes: Color shows radius minus the source map’s 255 km reference sphere. Brightness adds fixed northwest cartographic relief without height exaggeration. The model includes publisher-interpolated polar regions without a separate validity mask; those areas are not independent stereo observations. Shadows adds approximate fixed-epoch Sun lighting.

controls.label: Surface elements
controls.notes: Hydrogen in the top few decimetres of regolith, from epithermal neutrons counted by Dawn’s GRaND in its low orbit (Prettyman et al. 2012). One colour per archived 2-degree pixel, but each value blends about 300 km of surface, so the map is much blurrier than its pixels. Hydrogen is richest where dark, carbonaceous material fell on Vesta and poorest in the Rheasilvia basin. Moved from the archive’s Claudia Double Prime longitudes into the Claudia frame of the other maps.

facts.label: Reading the scale
facts.value: Micrograms of hydrogen per gram of regolith: 400 µg/g is 0.04% by weight.

facts.label: How it was measured
facts.value: Dawn’s gamma-ray and neutron detector counted epithermal neutrons from about 210 km above the surface, December 2011 to January 2012.

facts.label: Map detail
facts.value: Each archived pixel covers 2° of latitude and longitude; the instrument’s footprint is about 300 km across, so features smaller than that are not resolved.

facts.label: Limits
facts.value: The archive gives no uncertainty per pixel. Hydrogen may be bound in hydrated minerals; this is not a map of ice.

controls.label: Surface elements
controls.notes: How often Dawn’s GRaND detected the 7.6 MeV gamma rays that iron emits, corrected for the neutron density (Yamashita et al. 2013). A higher rate means more iron: basaltic eucrite terrain is richer than the diogenite excavated in the Rheasilvia basin. Values are archived on 0.5-degree equal-area pixels, but each blends about 300 km of surface. This is a counting rate, not an iron percentage; the authors’ preliminary factor of 189.2 wt% per count/s is not applied. Moved from Claudia Double Prime into the Claudia frame of the other maps.

facts.label: Reading the scale
facts.value: Counts per second of iron gamma rays in the detector. Higher means more iron; the scale is not a weight percent.

facts.label: How it was measured
facts.value: Dawn’s gamma-ray detector counted the 7.6 MeV iron line from about 210 km above the surface, December 2011 to April 2012, when pointed at Vesta.

facts.label: Map detail
facts.value: Pixels are 0.5° tall equal-area cells; the footprint is about 300 km across, so the map shows regional differences only.

facts.label: Limits
facts.value: The archive gives no uncertainty per pixel. Its catalogue gives a preliminary conversion to iron weight percent and advises caution; it is not used here.

controls.label: Surface elements
controls.notes: Fast neutrons counted by Dawn’s GRaND after removing the part that follows hydrogen (Lawrence et al. 2013). What is left follows the average atomic mass of the regolith: heavier, iron-rich basaltic eucrite reads higher than the diogenite of the Rheasilvia basin. The whole map spans only about 5%. One colour per archived pixel, 20 degrees tall. Moved from Claudia Double Prime into the Claudia frame of the other maps.

facts.label: Reading the scale
facts.value: Counts per second left after the hydrogen trend was removed. The level has an arbitrary offset, so only differences between places mean anything.

facts.label: How it was measured
facts.value: Dawn’s gamma-ray and neutron detector counted fast neutrons from about 210 km above the surface, December 2011 to January 2012 and April 2012.

facts.label: Map detail
facts.value: Pixels are 20° tall quasi-equal-area cells; the counts were smoothed over the detector footprint first, so the map shows only regional differences.

facts.label: Limits
facts.value: The archive gives no uncertainty per pixel; the authors say the smoothing makes it small. This is a counting rate, not a mass in atomic units.

controls.label: Surface elements
controls.notes: High-energy gamma rays counted by Dawn’s GRaND, corrected for background, viewing geometry and cosmic-ray changes (Peplowski et al. 2013). The rate rises with the heavy major elements in the top few tens of decimetres: eucrite-like terrain reads higher than the diogenite-like floor of Rheasilvia. One colour per archived pixel, 15 degrees tall, each blending about 300 km. Moved from Claudia Double Prime into the Claudia frame of the other maps.

facts.label: Reading the scale
facts.value: Counts per second of high-energy gamma rays in the detector. Higher means more heavy major elements; the scale is not a composition.

facts.label: How it was measured
facts.value: Dawn’s gamma-ray detector counted high-energy gamma rays from about 210 km above the surface, December 2011 to April 2012.

facts.label: Map detail
facts.value: Pixels are 15° tall quasi-equal-area cells; the footprint is about 300 km across, so the map shows regional differences only.

facts.label: Limits
facts.value: Each pixel’s 1-sigma uncertainty is 0.12 to 0.31 counts/s, a large part of the whole range, so neighbouring pixels can differ by noise alone.

controls.label: Surface elements
controls.notes: How strongly the regolith absorbs slow neutrons, from thermal and epithermal neutrons counted by Dawn’s GRaND (Prettyman et al. 2013). Absorption depends on Fe, Ca, Al, Mg and other rock-forming elements and rises with the share of basaltic eucrite: the Rheasilvia basin reads low, the dark hemisphere high. One colour per archived pixel, 15 degrees tall, each blending about 300 km. Moved from Claudia Double Prime into the Claudia frame of the other maps.

facts.label: Reading the scale
facts.value: The archived parameter DCP, which has no unit and rises in step with the neutron absorption cross section. Zero is not “no absorption”.

facts.label: How it was measured
facts.value: Dawn’s gamma-ray and neutron detector compared thermal and epithermal neutron counts from about 210 km above the surface, December 2011 to January 2012.

facts.label: Map detail
facts.value: Pixels are 15° tall quasi-equal-area cells; the footprint is about 300 km across, so the map shows regional differences only.

facts.label: Limits
facts.value: The archive gives a conversion to cross section that assumes howardite regolith; it is not applied. Each pixel’s 1-sigma uncertainty is 0.0014 to 0.0075.

controls.label: Gravity

legend.title: Radial gravity without J2
legend.meta: mGal on a 290 × 265 km ellipsoid · Dawn VESTA20H

controls.notes: How strongly Vesta pulls at each place: radial gravity on a 290 × 265 km ellipsoid close to the surface, from degrees 2 to 20 of the field without J2, its overall flattening. JPL maps radial gravity because the series does not converge on the geoid, so a true gravity anomaly cannot be computed. Milligals (mGal): 1 mGal is 0.00001 m/s², and Vesta's mean surface gravity is about 25,300 mGal. Red pulls harder and blue weaker; values beyond ±2,000 mGal (0.16% of the surface, in Vestalia Terra) use endpoint colors. JPL's Dawn gravity team fitted VESTA20H to Deep Space Network Doppler and range tracking and optical landmarks, July 2011 to July 2012 (Konopliv et al. 2014). The later degree-26 model VESTA26J (Park et al. 2025) is archived only as coefficients. Degree 20 corresponds to features about 42 km across at the 265 km reference radius; Raymond et al. (2013) call the field accurate to about degree 20. Each 1° cell holds the model value at its centre, moved from Claudia Double Prime into the Claudia frame of the other maps.

controls.label: Gravity

legend.title: Bouguer anomaly
legend.meta: mGal on a 290 × 265 km ellipsoid · degree 15

controls.notes: Radial gravity minus the pull the shape of Vesta would have at one uniform density: positive means denser material below. Raymond et al. (2013) describe a large positive anomaly at Vestalia Terra, a weaker one over the central mound of Rheasilvia and another over the equatorial troughs; all three read positive here. Milligals (mGal). Red marks extra mass below and blue a deficit. Values run from −156 to +238 mGal, inside the scale. JPL's Dawn gravity team fitted VESTA20H to Deep Space Network Doppler and range tracking and optical landmarks, July 2011 to July 2012 (Konopliv et al. 2014). The later degree-26 model VESTA26J (Park et al. 2025) is archived only as coefficients. The Bouguer map stops at degree 15, about 55 km, where JPL finds the Bouguer signal meets the model's error (the archive cites Konopliv et al. 2014, Section 4, Figure 5). Each 1° cell holds the model value at its centre, moved from Claudia Double Prime into the Claudia frame of the other maps.
